Marco Rubio: Saving Social Security in the 21st Century

When Social Security was created, the age at which one started to receive benefits was (purposely) set at the same age as average life expectancy. In other words, if you lived longer than average you got a little help to see you through. We need to return to that philosophy. If you live longer than average you get a small stipend to help cover your expenses. But, that is all Social Security should be--and, our desire to turn it into more than that is why it's failing.

This would actually cause it to function more like insurance, in that you would pay a modest amount to limit your risk of loss should an unlikely event occur (living far beyond the expected life expectancy). It would make far more economic sense than the current Ponzi-scheme.

my tax plan eliminates taxes on capital gains, interest and dividends

Thes right folks the way to save SS is to reduce the tax rate on the leisure rich, sitting poolside waiting for your hard work to pay them a dividends, to zero.

Warren buffet shouldn't pay a lower rate than his secretary, he should pay nothing!

Eliminating capital gains tax would benefit everyone. Those with large accumulations of capital would be incentivized to invest (which results in economic growth and jobs for others), and those looking to invest for retirement could much more easily do so. Sure, they may have access to current tax deferred retirement plans such as Roths, 401ks, IRAs, etc, but those present a great deal of risk to those in low economic quintiles because the money is essentially locked up until retirement. Though this is not a substantial problem to those with plenty of liquidity and steady cash flow, it's a huge problem for the bottom two quintiles where job loss or illness can cause catastrophic effects if their savings are locked up in a retirement plan they can't touch for decades.

I have seen a lot of discussion on Voat regarding Windows 10 and switching to Linux. Most of the comments discuss Debian flavors of Linux, but I have never seen anything mentioned regarding openSUSE, so I was wondering what the Voat community thought of it. When I gave my dad my old computer, I decided to keep Linux on it for many reasons, but especially so that it would be easy for me to maintain via SSH without having to go to his apartment. I decided to install Linux Mint on it because of Cinnamon being so similar to the Windows desktop. However, for my computers at home, I have run openSUSE for years, and I absolutely love it. Whenever I build a new computer, I find it easy to install (even when dual-booting with Windows). I love YaST (even more so than the tools on Linux Mint) and its update manager and package repositories. Everything seems to just work without a lot of tinkering, and I have found it to be very stable. I also like the business model behind it; I prefer to use a flavor of Linux that is developed alongside an enterprise version. Anyway, you've heard my arguments for it, and I have nothing against Debian flavors of Linux, but I was wondering what everyone else thinks of openSUSE?
